back: Micro-organisms such as Lactobacillus and others, commonly called LAB, that grow in milk and convert it to curd. During growth they produce acids that coagulate and partially digest the milk proteins.

A small amount of curd is added to fresh milk as inoculum or starter. It contains millions of LAB which multiply at suitable temperatures and convert milk to curd, improving nutritional quality by increasing vitamin B12.
In our stomach, LAB play a very beneficial role in checking disease-causing microbes.

front: Why dosa and idli dough puffs up
back: Bacteria ferment the dough and release CO2 gas, which gives the puffed-up appearance.
Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the yeast used to ferment bread dough. The same species, called brewer's yeast, ferments malted cereals and fruit juices to produce ethanol.
A traditional drink of some parts of southern India, made by fermenting sap from palms. Microbes are also used to ferment fish, soyabean and bamboo-shoots to make foods.
Its large holes are due to the production of a large amount of CO2 by the bacterium Propionibacterium sharmanii.
Ripened by growing a specific fungus on the cheese, which gives it a particular flavour.
Different varieties are known by their characteristic texture, flavour and taste, and the specificity comes from the microbes used. Cheese is one of the oldest food items in which microbes were used.
A very large vessel in which microbes are grown for production on an industrial scale.

front: Alcoholic drinks: with and without distillation
back: Wine and beer are produced without distillation, whereas whisky, brandy and rum are produced by distillation of the fermented broth. The drink obtained also depends on the raw material fermented.
Chemical substances which are produced by some microbes and can kill or retard the growth of other (disease-causing) microbes.
Anti is Greek for 'against' and bio means 'life' — together 'against life' in the context of disease-causing organisms. With reference to human beings they are 'pro life', not against.

Alexander Fleming saw a mould growing in an unwashed culture plate of Staphylococci, with no Staphylococci around it. The mould produced a chemical he named penicillin, after Penicillium notatum. Chain and Florey later established its full potential, and all three shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.
Citric acid — Aspergillus niger (fungus); acetic acid — Acetobacter aceti; butyric acid — Clostridium butylicum; lactic acid — Lactobacillus.
Lipases are used in detergent formulations to remove oily stains from the laundry. Pectinases and proteases clarify bottled fruit juices, which is why they look clearer than home-made juice.

Produced by the bacterium Streptococcus and modified by genetic engineering; used as a 'clot buster' to remove clots from the blood vessels of patients who have had a myocardial infarction leading to heart attack.
A bioactive molecule produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum, used as an immunosuppressive agent in organ-transplant patients.
Produced by the yeast Monascus purpureus and commercialised as blood-cholesterol lowering agents. They act by competitively inhibiting the enzyme responsible for synthesis of cholesterol.
Municipal waste water, of which human excreta is a major component. It contains large amounts of organic matter and microbes, many of which are pathogenic.
Heterotrophic microbes naturally present in the sewage. Treatment is carried out in two stages — primary (physical) and secondary (biological).

Physical removal of particles by filtration and sedimentation: floating debris is removed by sequential filtration, then grit (soil and small pebbles) by sedimentation. Settled solids form the primary sludge; the supernatant is the effluent.
Masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments forming mesh-like structures, which grow vigorously in the aerated tank and consume the major part of the organic matter in the effluent.

The amount of oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one litre of water were oxidised by bacteria. The BOD test measures the rate of uptake of oxygen by micro-organisms, so BOD is an indirect measure of the organic matter present. The greater the BOD, the greater the polluting potential.
The sediment of bacterial flocs formed in the settling tank after aeration. A small part is pumped back into the aeration tank as the inoculum; the rest goes to anaerobic sludge digesters.

Bacteria growing anaerobically digest the bacteria and fungi of the sludge and release a mixture of methane, hydrogen sulphide and carbon dioxide. These gases form biogas, which is inflammable and usable as a source of energy.

Bacteria that grow anaerobically on cellulosic material and produce a large amount of methane along with CO2 and H2. A common example is Methanobacterium. They occur in anaerobic sludge and in the rumen of cattle.
They help in the breakdown of cellulose in the rumen, playing an important role in the nutrition of cattle. Cattle dung (gobar) is therefore rich in these bacteria and is used to generate gobar gas.

A concrete tank 10-15 feet deep in which bio-wastes are collected and a slurry of dung is fed. A floating cover rises as gas is produced, an outlet and pipe supply biogas to nearby houses, and the spent slurry leaves through another outlet and is used as fertiliser.

front: Who developed biogas technology in India
back: The Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) and the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC).
The use of biological methods for controlling plant diseases and pests — natural predation and microbial pathogens instead of insecticides and pesticides.

front: Why organic farmers do not eradicate pests
back: Pests are kept at manageable levels by checks and balances in the ecosystem. Eradicating them is undesirable, because the beneficial predatory and parasitic insects that depend on them as food or hosts would not survive.
The ladybird, the familiar beetle with red and black markings, gets rid of aphids; dragonflies get rid of mosquitoes.

A microbial biocontrol agent supplied as dried spores in sachets, mixed with water and sprayed on vulnerable plants such as brassicas and fruit trees. The larvae eat the spores, the toxin is released in the gut, and the larvae are killed; other insects are left unharmed.
A plant into which B. thuringiensis toxin genes have been introduced by genetic engineering, making it resistant to attack by insect pests. It is cultivated in some states of India.
Free-living fungi very common in root ecosystems, effective as biocontrol agents of several plant pathogens. A biological control being developed for use in the treatment of plant disease.

Pathogens that attack insects and other arthropods, mostly of the genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus. They are species-specific and narrow spectrum, with no negative impacts shown on plants, mammals, birds, fish or non-target insects — useful in IPM programmes and ecologically sensitive areas.
Organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil. The main sources are bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria.

Rhizobium fixes atmospheric nitrogen symbiotically in the root nodules of leguminous plants, converting it into organic forms used by the plant. Azospirillum and Azotobacter fix nitrogen while free-living in the soil.

A symbiotic association of fungi with plant roots; many members of the genus Glomus form it. The fungal symbiont absorbs phosphorus from the soil and passes it to the plant, and the association also gives resistance to root-borne pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought, and better plant growth.

Autotrophic microbes widely distributed in aquatic and terrestrial environments, many of which fix atmospheric nitrogen — Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria. In paddy fields they serve as an important biofertiliser, and the blue green algae also add organic matter to the soil and increase its fertility.

Plans initiated by the Ministry of Environment and Forests to save these rivers from pollution, proposing to build a large number of sewage treatment plants so that only treated sewage is discharged into them.
